title: Fireworks.ai Update on October 2026 security incident
content:
The update
This is an update to our previous security bulletin published on October 9, 2026. In response to the incident, we notified law enforcement and obtained assistance from a leading cybersecurity firm, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, to help conduct forensic analysis. At the time of publishing the bulletin, only Fireworks stored secrets (e.g. used in evaluation jobs) were known to have been accessed. Since then, we discovered impacts to account and billing information. For a limited set of accounts, we also discovered impact to secrets, datasets, and incomplete models.
The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways, known as "LLMJacking". On November 2, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published a blog post about the rise of LLMJacking, their motives, techniques used, and mitigation.
Further activity
A third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks R&D machines experienced a security incident on October 23. On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact. We detected this activity on the same day, and followed our incident response processes to take immediate remediation measures and close known critical vulnerabilities. As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use.
Data involved
The affected internal application provided access to the following categories of information:
- Resource metadata, such as Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation time, etc.
- Billing information, such as billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage. Payment card numbers are not stored by Fireworks and were not impacted.
- Model weights and datasets, for certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed.
We are notifying customers whose data was impacted, and providing details about the impact and recommended response actions.
We have not detected any impact to Inference, Training SDK and Nexus, which are all zero data retention (ZDR) by default. These findings are based on our investigation to date. Our investigation is ongoing and may reveal additional information.
What we have done
Working with Unit 42, Fireworks identified and implemented security hardening procedures, including:
- Access and credential lockdown. Fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, removed unnecessary elevated privileges, and tightened controls designed to prevent new unauthorized credentials from being created.
- Network isolation. Fireworks restricted unauthorized network pathways and isolated affected systems designed to prevent further unauthorized activity and movement between systems.
- Data protection. Fireworks reviewed and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems and enforced controls designed to prevent public or unauthorized access to stored data.
- Forensic and audit integrity. Fireworks secured and enhanced our logging and monitoring systems.
As part of our response, we’ve disabled self-serve dataset uploads and downloads used by Batch Inference and dataset-based training while we investigate this incident. Training SDK remains available with ZDR, i.e. no training data stored at rest, and Fireworks Lab-based training operates in an isolated environment with additional network and storage protection. We continue to work with Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 on our investigation and security hardening.
We will continue to monitor our systems 24/7 and will provide further updates on our investigation as appropriate.
Contact
Reply to your incident notification email or contact security-notice@fireworks.ai

report.summary: Fireworks.ai disclosed that the October 2026 breach, linked to an LLMJacking crew, exposed customer billing data, datasets and some model weights after attackers pivoted through a compromised third-party cloud provider.
report.background: AI inference providers sit on high-value assets: API keys that unlock metered access to frontier models. A criminal economy has grown around stealing those credentials and reselling the resulting capacity through grey-market routing gateways, a practice Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant catalogued as 'LLMJacking'. Fireworks.ai, a major serverless inference and fine-tuning platform, first disclosed an incident on October 9, 2026, initially scoped to its own internal secrets. The company engaged Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensics and notified law enforcement. Scope widened in late October when a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks R&D machines was itself compromised, giving attackers a bridge into Fireworks development environments. The case illustrates how AI infrastructure companies inherit supply-chain risk from hosting providers, and how stolen compute and model weights, not just personal data, have become the target.
key_points: Scope grew well beyond the first bulletin. What began as exposure of Fireworks' own internal secrets expanded to account and billing records (addresses, invoices, payment history, balances) for many customers, plus secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights for a limited set of accounts. Card numbers were not stored and were not affected.

The entry path was a supplier, not Fireworks directly. A third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks R&D machines was breached on October 23; on October 24 attackers used that foothold to reach development machines and run an unauthorised workload. Fireworks says it detected and remediated the same day.

The likely motive is reselling model access. Evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group that sells tokens obtained through unauthorised LLM access to illicit routing gateways, the pattern known as LLMJacking. Fireworks cites a joint Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant post published November 2.

Customer-facing inference appears untouched. Fireworks says Inference, the Training SDK and Nexus are zero data retention by default and show no detected impact. Self-serve dataset upload and download for Batch Inference and dataset-based training were suspended during the investigation.

Remediation focused on credential and network containment. Actions included revoking and rotating credentials and service accounts, removing excess privileges, blocking unauthorised network paths, isolating affected systems, tightening storage access and strengthening logging for forensic integrity.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a template for a new class of incident: the stolen asset is not just personal data but model weights, fine-tuning datasets and API credentials that can be monetised at scale. Expect investors and enterprise buyers to demand supplier-risk disclosure and stronger isolation between an AI vendor's production and R&D estates. For developers, the practical lesson is that platform-side protections do not extend to your own artefacts: proprietary datasets and partially trained checkpoints uploaded to third-party tooling are exposed exactly like any other cloud data. Teams should assume secrets stored in evaluation jobs or CI pipelines may leak and should rotate keys, prefer zero-retention endpoints and keep sensitive weights in their own accounts. For regular users, direct harm is limited to billing and address data, but availability of self-serve dataset features may be disrupted.
report.tools: Follow Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 and Google Threat Intelligence Group/Mandiant publications on LLMJacking for indicators and mitigations. For hygiene, use secret scanners such as Gitleaks and TruffleHog in CI, a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS for key rotation, and egress monitoring via Falco, Wazuh or cloud-native flow logs to catch unexpected model API calls. Cloud security posture tools like Prowler and Steampipe help audit third-party accounts, while AI gateways with per-key budgets and anomaly alerts make stolen-token abuse easier to spot.
